Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

Amazon workers at the Port St. Lucie fulfillment center will be paid for the last time Sept. 17 as the facility begins a two-year renovation, with local leaders working to help the displaced employees transition to new opportunities. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 “Obviously, the greatest impact is on the workers and their families,” said Wicker Perlis, spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council. Since the closure was announced in May, county officials tell WPBF 25 News that many employees have successfully transferred to other Amazon locations or found work with new employers. “We can say at this point that a majority of the employees who were there in May, easily a majority, have found new work by the time the closure took place,” Perlis said. The EDC partnered with CareerSource Research Coast and local businesses to assist workers in finding new jobs. CareerSource organized hiring events and job assistance programs specifically for the displaced Amazon employees, bringing in companies such as Walmart, CVS and Pursuit Aero to connect with workers. Walmart interviewed dozens of employees and hired 25. Import Mex hired 12 workers and is considering others for future openings, while CVS Distribution hired two. Additionally, four reemployment sessions were held, reaching over 100 affected workers with information on job placement services, training programs and other resources. County officials said the timing of new employers and expanding businesses helped create options for many of the people looking for their next paycheck. “There are jobs out there. And we can try and help you, connect you with a good job,” Perlis said. Amazon has announced that the renovated facility is expected to reopen in 2028 with about 1,000 employees. Until then, officials said the focus remains on ensuring those impacted by the temporary closure have a plan for what is next. According to CareerSource Research Coast, the fulfillment center has been closed since Sept. 6, and affected workers are still being paid on time until Sept. 17, when their employment will be officially terminated. (AP) — In the mind of Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over. It happened in May, in a far-from-filled Swedish arena, when Barkov suited up for Finland in an exhibition against Switzerland for his first game since shredding his right knee in the Panthers' first training camp practice 7 1/2 months earlier. And on one of his very first shifts, he tumbled to the ice. “Very good news,” Barkov said. That was all it took for Barkov to realize his surgically repaired knee was good, that he could play without fear or concern. A few weeks later, he hoisted the trophy when Finland won the IIHF world championship. And now he's home in Florida, set for the start of training camp and ready to lead a team that — even after missing the playoffs last season — has been set by most sportsbooks as the favorite to win what would be its third Stanley Cup in a four-year span. “Don't take anything for granted,” Barkov said, when asked what he learned from not being able to play for Florida last season. “You just have to enjoy every single chance you get to play hockey, to be with your teammates, to go to every single practice, every single game. You’ve got to be excited about that.” The Panthers — who were holding media day on Wednesday in advance of Thursday's first practice of camp — have plenty of reasons to be excited. Many core players from the runs to the Cup titles in 2024 and 2025 are back, names like Barkov, Matthew Tkachuk, Sam Reinhart, Sam Bennett, Aaron Ekblad, Carter Verhaeghe, Gustav Forsling, Brad Marchand, Anton Lundell, Dmitry Kulikov and Niko Mikkola. Brady Tkachuk, Matthew Tkachuk's brother, has been added to the mix and Florida even brought Radko Gudas — a fan favorite from his first stint with the Panthers — back to help shore up the defense. And in net, with Sergei Bobrovsky gone to Toronto, Florida is turning the goaltender job over to Jacob Markstrom. “Every single guy who has come in, they look so determined to be their best and to show their best," Barkov said. “But they also know that we’re all in this together. Every single person is important, and every single has their own abilities to lead in their own way. We have many of those guys, so that’s the best part of this. No one’s here by themselves. Everyone can be just whatever they are.” That didn't happen last season. Injuries gutted the Panthers, starting with Barkov. He got hurt about 20 minutes into the first practice of training camp, tearing the ACL and MCL in his right knee on Sept. He had surgery a day later and was skating within a few months, but by the time he was ready to seriously consider returning to game action Florida — which dealt with injuries all year — was out of playoff contention and didn't get a chance at trying to win a third consecutive Stanley Cup. It wasn't entirely a lost season for Barkov. He missed the chance to serve as Finland's captain at the Milan Cortina Olympics, but played for his country at the IIHF world championships this past spring — and got to hoist the trophy when Finland beat host Switzerland 1-0 in the gold medal game. And now, Florida's career leader in goals and assists is raring to go with the Panthers once again. “We all know camp is always going to be hard, no matter what. It's going to be hard physically and mentally," Barkov said. "We're all kind of ready for that test.” ___ See AP’s full NHL coverage here

Flock cameras helped track down a burglary suspect in Vero Beach , according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office . IRCSO says that Guy Keith Tibbetts II, 44, was arrested on Sept. 6 after an allegedly burglary at a home on Reef Road in Vero Beach. According to the affidavit, deputies were called when the homeowner who was out of town at the time saw an unknown man inside of his home via his surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man, later identified as Tibbetts, wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves showing up at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed Tibbetts inside of the home with a flashlight and a tote bag. He could be seen opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door, IRCSO says. The items taking were estimated to be valued at around $1,010. See also: 'I killed my mom': No bond for man charged in mother's stabbing death in west Delray Beach Deputies collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door. Investigators also used the homeowner’s description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, the affidavit said. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to Tibbett's apartment complex. After being read his rights, Tibbetts allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission, according to the affidavit. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on reef road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage, and he was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, and grand theft between $750 and $5,000, along with another theft charge.

More details have emerged regarding the Fort Pierce man who was found with several military-grade explosives inside of his home. According to the arrest affidavit, SLCSO deputies served Keith Anthony Morrone with a temporary risk protection order at his Balsam Drive residence in Fort Pierce. Morrone allowed deputies to search his vehicle and his residence, where they found green wooden case with 7 items that resembled military style hand grenades. Five of the items were deemed to be more consistent with flash bangs. After everyone including Morrone evacuated the residence, the SLCSO bomb team was called in to handle the situation. See also: Boca Raton woman charged after allegedly hurling stones at occupied vehicles, police say While talking with deputies, Morrone admitted to modifying the grenades, according to the affidavit. When asked if there was anything inside of the grenades, Morrone said I don’t know, I don’t think there’s anything in there, SLCSO says. The explosives were eventually safely removed from the house, but another search of the home discovered one foot of canon fuse connected to a small glass container containing black powder, creating a home-made destructive device. Based on the evidence, Morrone was charged with 8 counts of making, possessing, throwing, projecting, placing, or discharging any destructive device or attempting to do so.

Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the development. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million — $15 million more than previously planned. WATCH BELOW: Developers of Kings Landing given 6 months to fund hotel Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant, but were denied. Now, Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will look to secure the funds privately. "We can get it done," Collier said. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed. "With millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, we're extremely motivated to see this through to a successful completion," the representative said. The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. "My opinion, based on the legal review of this, is that we need to stop now. Because if we do another amendment, it continues to weaken us and makes it more difficult to get the property back," Dzadovsky said. On Tuesday, WPTV sat down with Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension. Broderick said taking back the property — currently owned by Audubon Development — would be costly and lead to litigation. "Everybody's going to be suing everybody. It's like having three fighters in the same ring, and they're all going to come out swinging at each other," Broderick said. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick was direct. "I'm going to kick them to the curb. I'll make the motion to terminate the deal," Broderick said. Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. "If this is really what it takes and they can find the money to be able to do this, great. Then we can get moving forward," Nolli said. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays. "If this is just another step extending it along, that's going to be pretty tough on everybody," Nolli said. A West Palm Beach woman has been arrested more than a year after a 7-vehicle crash killed a 71-year-old man in Palm Beach County.Elizabeth Marie Romero Diaz, 46, was arrested at approximately 11:09 p.m. 15 with assistance from the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Warrants Unit. She is charged with one count of manslaughter by culpable negligence.The charge stems from a July 15, 2025 crash near the intersection of South Military Trail and Westgate Avenue.Investigators said Diaz was driving a Mazda SUV when she approached traffic stopped at a red light and failed to stop, slow down or take evasive action. Her SUV struck the back of a Chevrolet SUV, triggering a chain-reaction crash involving several other vehicles.The crash killed Louis A. Vanegas-Valez, 71, just 5 days before his 72nd birthday. 2 other drivers were injured and taken to nearby hospitals for treatment.

WPTV is getting answers for Delray Beach residents who say a federally mandated pipe replacement project could leave them facing thousands of dollars in costs, with some homeowners still searching for clarity on how they'll pay for it.A Delray Beach woman who brought her concerns directly to WPTV through the station's Let's Hear It community event says she could be on the hook for as much as $13,000 to replace water service lines on her property as part of a citywide infrastructure project.Jayne Milner has lived in her Delray Beach home for about 30 years. She said she supports updating aging infrastructure but became concerned after learning homeowners may be responsible for replacing portions of service lines located on private property."This is the letter from the city of Delray Beach," Milner said, holding up the notice she received from the city.Milner told WPTV she reached out to city officials after receiving the notification but was left with more questions than answers.According to Milner, she was trying to understand not only who would pay for the work but also what financial assistance might be available."And they didn't really have any direct answers," she said.Milner said she started gathering estimates from plumbers and was surprised by the cost."When I got some estimates, I didn't feel that great because it's kind of expensive," she said.When asked about the estimates she received, Milner replied, "Let's say from $5,000 to $13,000 for different plumbers to replace the pipes."She said the price tag was far more than she expected.WPTV turned to the city of Delray Beach for answers and learned the project stems from new Environmental Protection Agency regulations known as the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, which require water utilities across the country to identify and replace certain types of water service lines that could potentially contribute to lead exposure.According to information provided by the city, approximately 2,100 city-owned service lines and about 3,000 customer-owned service lines may ultimately require replacement. The city says those figures are still being verified.A service line is the pipe that brings water from the city's water main to a home or business. Generally, the city owns the portion between the water main and the water meter, while property owners are responsible for the portion between the meter and the building.The city says if a customer-owned service line falls under the federal replacement requirements, the homeowner will be required to replace that section.For Milner, the uncertainty has been frustrating."I was hoping that something would happen, but nothing. I haven't heard anything, so I thought, well, maybe I'll come here and talk about it and then we can get some more information," she said at our Let's Hear It event.She believes many of her neighbors share the same concerns."I feel that since they are replacing (the pipes) they should offer some kind of assistance. I talked to my neighbors, and they thought that was too expensive for them to be putting out, but we have a lot of retirees and working people, and they felt that it was a bit too much of a burden," Milner said.Milner lives in a neighborhood with more than 200 homes and worries many residents may struggle to absorb the cost."Well, I don't know really what the solution is except for to get some kind of assistance because it is a lot and if they're going to be replacing throughout the city, I think they should have some kind of budget requirement," Milner added.The city told WPTV it is currently exploring potential funding options, including federal and state grants, low-interest loans, cost-sharing programs, rebates and other forms of financial assistance. However, no assistance program has been finalized.Milner said she also wants more information about how the project will affect residents moving forward."Just how long it's going to last and when are they going to start and what kind of impact it's going to have on our individual homes," she said.Milner also wants to know what happens if homeowners cannot afford the work."Yes, and also what would be the problem if we didn't replace them," she said.The city says affected property owners will receive direct notification if their service line requires replacement. Residents will also receive information about timelines, requirements and any financial assistance programs that become available.The EPA's regulations take effect Nov. 1, 2027, and replacement programs are generally required to be completed by Dec. The city says work will be completed in phases over several years and residents will receive advance notice before construction begins in their neighborhoods.The city also says property owners who do not complete a required replacement will be given notice and an opportunity to comply before any enforcement action is considered.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A man has been arrested after surveillance footage captured him violently abusing a service dog in two separate incidents along South Federal Highway, Boynton Beach police said.Juan Latrez Poole, 52, was arrested on Monday, on a felony animal cruelty charge, police said.Last Wednesday, officers said they responded to the 2300 block of South Federal Highway after a witness reported seeing a man lift a black lab above his head and slam it to the ground near a bus stop outside a Taco Bell. The dog, later identified as Rex, was wearing a red "service dog" vest and appeared to weigh approximately 50 pounds, police said. Officers were unable to locate the man or the dog at the time.The following morning, on Sept. 10, a second witness reported a nearly identical incident just blocks away, police said. The caller told police she watched a man choke the same black lab with its leash, lift the dog off the ground, swing it through the air, and strike it with a water bottle. The caller stated the dog was visibly terrified, shaking and cowering, according to police.Boynton Beach Police Department's Animal Control Officer canvassed the area and recovered surveillance footage that captured both incidents, police said. In the first video, the Poole is seen lifting the dog completely off the ground, and at one point inverting the animal upside down in mid-air, before slamming it to the ground, police said. In the second video, he is seen yanking the leash, striking the dog with a bottle, and hoisting the dog several feet into the air by its neck before dropping it to the ground.Poole was later identified by a witness in a photo lineup and was arrested by Boynton Beach police. He is currently being held at the Palm Beach County Jail on $30,000 bond.Rex was transported to Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control and is currently looking for his forever home, police said.

We're now a few weeks into the new school year and we're highlighting the amazing things teachers are doing in the lives of your students. CBS12 News’ next Teacher Feature within the Martin County School District is said to be a great model for the relatively new co-teaching initiative being rolled out at certain schools. Kevin Kobold is a geometry co-teacher at South Fork High School in Stuart. "Okay, so like usually there's like 28 to 29 kids in the classroom. So if there's one teacher trying to instruct to 29 minds in there, you might lose half of them. So if we split it in half, and now it's a ratio of like 15 to one, you're really able to engage with the students more and really like focus on some kids that are struggling, said Kabold. "I'm helping take a lot off her weight that she doesn't have to be up there instructing from bell to bell every class. I can be doing the same thing too. So, getting to know your co-teacher and knowing your role in the classroom, I think, is key there. And also being able to like finish each other's sentences, like what we do in there." Kabold knows geometry can be difficult to a lot of students and really focuses on making his lessons interesting and fun, rather than just note-taking. "So, if we're working on notes, they're usually like guided notes where they're not having to write two pages of their own handwriting. That's when you'll lose a lot of the kids. So we use the whiteboards. We have stations set up, said Kabold. "We're reviewing for a test on Friday, so we're really having them engage with the material to try to get it to stick a little more than just sitting there and doing a review on the computer." See also: 'We were ready': One family's journey to keeping foster brothers together District officials said that students really respect Kabold, which he says is really important to gain early on. "I mean, like when you gain that rapport with students, and they kind of find out that you're there for them and you truly do care about them, they will open up a little more, and they will try harder than just you know sitting back there and not asking them about, 'Hey how'd your football game go?' Or, 'hey how'd your band practice go?' said Kabold. Like once you get to know them and know what they do out of the classroom, then you see like their eyes light up, and now they want to come in class." Kabold says while he knows geometry isn’t the most fun class, there is one big message he wants his students to leave with. "If you learn some geometry, that's amazing. I want you to do well on your EOC. But this is really about solving problems that come up in your life when you're given certain information. How am I going to solve this problem? I really try to make it real life for them because let's be real, a lot of them may not have a career that requires them to remember the Pythagorean theorem or something from geometry, but they're going to be faced with issues in their life, and I don't want them to just hide from them. So just try in our classroom, be present, and you'll learn something. I promise." Co-teaching has been used in Martin County middle and high school over the past few years. This is only the second year at South Fork High. District officials say co-teaching is about to be introduced in elementary schools, but didn't specify when. Florida's largest dude ranch is hiding in plain sight — and you don't have to cross the Mississippi to get the full wild west experience.WATCH BELOW: Inside Florida's largest dude ranch: Westgate River Ranch Resort and RodeoWestgate River Ranch Resort and Rodeo sits on more than 1,000 acres in River Ranch, nestled in Polk County. Centrally located between both coasts and just 90 miles south of Orlando, it's an easy trip for most Floridians."Where else can you go and then all of a sudden just disappear from the hustle and bustle of town, and whammo you're here on a ranch — an active ranch," General Manager Jim Szabo said.And active is an understatement. Szabo's days can look very different from one hour to the next."I can be in the field helping a cow give birth at three in the morning and then a few hours later I'm meeting guests at the front desk," Szabo said.Guests are encouraged to have fun and play. Activities include horseback riding, an adventure park, archery, axe throwing, and paintball. The brand new River Country Waterpark offers a way to cool off on hot days."We have archery, axe throwing, we have a paintball right back there," Szabo said.When the sun goes down, guests don't have to rough it. Westgate River Ranch offers a range of well-appointed accommodations — including glamping tents and Conestoga wagons — that bring luxury to the outdoors."When we say glamping here at the Ranch, we mean glamping — this is luxury. So come on, let's take a look," Szabo said. "How many teepees come with fireplaces?"The Conestoga wagons sleep up to 6, feature a full-sized bathroom, and are climate controlled. Guests also receive a personal concierge and hot brewed coffee delivered every morning."Everything you could possibly want in a luxury hotel room — in a tent. Again, absolutely amazing," Szabo said.When it's time to eat, there's something for every palate — from fine dining at the Cattle Company Chophouse to Rodeo Ray's Pizzeria. And after dinner, the cowboy donuts are a must."The campfire right here is a s'mores donut with the chocolate, graham crackers, and marshmallow — you can have that toasted. So we will actually have the little toaster and you can toast the top of the marshmallows, if you like," Szabo said.It's easy to see why the resort was recently named one of the nation's best glamping spots by USA Today.But the real ranch experience, Szabo said, happens outside — not inside."One thing you aren't going to find in any of these rooms is a TV set. The idea is to disconnect," Szabo said. "The idea is even at nighttime you don't want to be here — you want to be sitting out creating that story at the campfire.""This is when you come to reconnect and to actually get that experience with your family that a lot of people don't get anymore," Szabo said.Every Saturday night, the resort hosts a professional rodeo — adding one more reason to stay through the weekend."Look — there's two types of vacation and two types of stories. You can go on a vacation where you are not the hero of that story. Here at Westgate Ranch, we are the heroes of the story because what we're sending you home with is a lifetime of memories that you're not going to get anywhere else," Szabo said.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

Florida shoppers are paying more for grocery essentials than residents in most other states, according to a new study — and local shoppers say they feel it every time they head to the store.An analysis by Self Financial compared 30 essential grocery items, including meat, milk, eggs and produce and found Florida's basket costs $134.35 — about $2 more than the national average. The study found that the Sunshine State ranks eighth most expensive in the country for the cost of essentials.On Wednesday, I spoke with shoppers about how they stretch their grocery dollars.Elaine Capute said looking for deals at the grocery store is a full-time job."I go online for the Publix ad. I clip all the digital coupons because you never know what you're going to buy," Capute said. "I don't know what people do that work full time, because it really takes up a lot of my time, but we're retired, and I do what I have to do."Retired chef Monte Schrier said his go-to strategy is shopping at a wholesaler, where he gets deals as a member. He showed me his last receipt, where 40 pounds of bulk chicken breasts cost just $1.39 a pound."Clean it, cut it, cryo-vac it and freeze it. A lot of people don't like to do that. They don't like to freeze stuff, but if you want to pay $6 a pound every time," Schrier said.Schrier said he also shops around, hitting two or three stores and getting the best deals at each.For shopper Betty Magar, the strategy is planning ahead."I eat for that week, what's on sale or what's a BOGO," Magar said.Shopper Bryce Hipp said with a fourth child on the way, the priority is making sure his kids have plenty."Take a look at what we eat versus what our kids eat. We want our kids to not go without anything. Sometimes we might dial back what we might want," Hipp said.Food prices continue to fluctuate. Uncooked turkey and other poultry are up 11.5% in the past year, and instant coffee is up 11%. Egg prices, however, are down 23% over the past year.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Dolly Parton's Imagination Library is experiencing a surge in donations and new registrations in Palm Beach County following her death, as the community rallies to carry on her legacy of early childhood literacy.Monique Boothe, a mother of 4, signed her children up for the program nearly a year ago. WATCH BELOW: Donations, registrations spike for Dolly's Imagination Library"It feels like Christmas every month because they get so excited they don't know what book they are going to get," Boothe said.Thanks to the program, her kids are getting less screen time and are learning the value of books and how to read.When Parton died, Boothe's kids were worried about what would happen to their monthly book deliveries."He was like, 'We get her books all the time; is that going to stop?'" Boothe said.Her kids look forward to getting the books in the mail because they have their name on it. The program is allowing them to build up their at-home library. "They bring it to me and say, 'Mommy, can you read it to me?' And they look at the pictures, and they are smiling," Boothe said.Roxanne Mutchler, a board member with Palm Beach County's Imagination Library, said the program's legacy will continue."We had over 200 new children registered to get the books, which has to be a record for us. Not only have registrations gone up, but so have the donations," Mutchler said.Participation in the Imagination Library allows families to build an at-home library of up to 60 books before their child starts kindergarten, at no cost to the family, regardless of income. Books are high-quality and age-appropriate, selected by a panel of experts for each age group. Each book also includes caregiver reading resources to maximize engagement.The program currently serves West Palm Beach, Lake Park, Mangonia Park, Riviera Beach and western Palm Beach County, among other areas, with coverage expanding to additional cities as funding is secured. The operational cost to support that coverage is $2.60 per book, including postage.The program is made possible through community support. Their next major fundraiser will be the Dolly Parton Imagination Library 5K Walk or Run.

Amazon has laid off roughly 300 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center as the facility prepares to shut down for renovations, with more employees transferred to other Amazon sites. Since the company filed a WARN notice in July listing 494 affected workers, Amazon says more than 200 additional employees have transferred to other facilities. Workers who aren't transferring will begin receiving paid severance this month. Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, as required under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy, effective Thursday, September 17. Roughly 494 employees will be separated from the company, with separations effective September 17 and December 17. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18, according to the filing. The job cuts are expected to be permanent, the notice states. Affected employees aren't represented by a union and don't have seniority-based "bumping rights" to displace other workers. Amazon says it will pay employees through their separation date, provided they don't resign early, and will share benefits and severance information separately. The vast majority of the affected positions 466 of the 494 are "FC Associate I" roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles, according to a list attached to the filing. Local economic development officials say that reduced number didn't happen by accident. Lucie Economic Development Council says the facility typically employs between 850 and 1,000 workers depending on the season. In the four months before Amazon filed the WARN notice, CareerSource Research Coast and the EDC held weekly job fairs and helped place many affected workers with other area employers, including Costco, Cheney Brothers and ImportMex, which the EDC says brought the number of employees ultimately listed in the WARN filing down to 494. Amazon describes the closure differently than the legal notice does. In a statement shortly after the notice, company spokesperson Amber Plunkett said, "The Treasure Coast is a great place to live and work, and we're proud of our partnerships across St. These investments and improvements reflect our long-term confidence in the region." On the Port St. Lucie facility specifically, Plunkett said, "We're always evaluating our network to make sure it fits our business needs and to improve the experience for our employees, customers, partners, and drivers. As part of that effort, we occasionally convert existing facilities to a new type of facility which is what we plan to do here later this year. When these renovations are done, Port St. Lucie will be home to a new fulfilment center that will create long-term benefits for our customers, employees, and the community for many years to come." On what happens to the facility's workers, Plunkett said, "Our goal is to keep all of our employees based at this facility with Amazon. Our HR team will work with everyone to offer transfers to another location that fits their preferences we have 30 facilities across South Florida. For those who prefer not to transfer, we'll be providing transition support. When this facility reopens in mid-to-late 2028, it will employ approximately 1,000 people, and everyone from the site will have the option to return at that time." Amazon says the project represents a $200 million investment in the South Florida region. The company says operations will shift to other nearby facilities during the closure and that customers won't be affected. Amazon also said it's working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations a figure that doesn't match the roughly 494 workers listed as affected in the WARN filing. It's not clear from the materials Amazon provided how the two numbers relate. Employees have the option to transfer to two nearby facilities specifically, or to any of the company's roughly 30 sites across South Florida, and Amazon says it's offering relocation bonuses to employees who transfer more than 50 miles from Port St. All employees affected by this closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens, according to Amazon. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend called the closure part of a bigger strain on businesses in the county. It's devastating," Townsend said. Townsend said the impact will ripple beyond the workers who lost their jobs. "They rent, they eat in restaurants, their children go to daycare, they go to our schools," Townsend said. "And so it's going to ripple down. It is going to hurt the economy here in Saint Lucie County. And I have concerns for those families. And jobs are not plentiful right here in this county." Townsend credited the EDC's job-placement efforts with softening the blow, but said the layoffs point to a broader pattern of job insecurity in the county. She said local leaders should focus on attracting small businesses that are more likely to stay rooted in the community rather than larger corporations. "They're the fabric of what makes up our community," Townsend said. "And they live here, and they pay taxes here. And we need to do what we have to do to make them successful, not be worried about the big box stores, because these are things that can happen."

Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

Lucie parent is calling for changes to a school bus stop near Paar Drive and Winslow Street, saying students are forced to walk along portions of the road where there is no sidewalk.Belinda Green said she became concerned about the safety of students using the specific bus stop and shared a video on TikTok showing the area.WATCH: Port St. Lucie parent raises safety concerns over bus stop“This is an easy resolve, make two stops,” Green said.She tells WPTV her biggest concern is the limited space available for students walking along Paar Drive.“That's the white line for the car... that shouldn't be for a human being,” Green said.Green suggests splitting the stops in the area so students have less distance to walk along the roadway. Instead of having students use only the bus stop at Paar Drive and Winslow Street, she would like to see an additional bus stop at Paar Drive and Jarmer Road. She says that could help prevent students from having to walk along a narrow stretch of roadway and cross the street after the bus has already left.“One little slip up — and we are looking at a tragedy unfolding,” Green said.WPTV reached out to St. Lucie Public Schools about Green's concerns.The district said its transportation department reviewed all routes and bus stops in the area and determined the existing stops are appropriate for student use.But after WPTV brought Green's concerns to the district, the school district made a change to one route nearby.Officials said a route change nearby was made to reduce the need for students to cross the road, while students who do need to cross should do so under the direction of the bus driver and with the bus's safety control devices.Green said she believes addressing potential safety concerns now is better than waiting for a serious incident.“I'd rather we find a resolution now than one day we have hashtags or there's a GoFundMe for some child or parent's funeral fund,” Green said.

Lucie County Sheriff’s Office arrested a Fort Pierce man after deputies found what they believe were multiple destructive devices at his home Thursday. According to the sheriff’s office, at about 12:20 p.m. Thursday, detectives with the SLCSO Targeted Violence Unit were serving a risk protection order at the home, located near Balsam Drive, when they identified numerous suspected destructive devices. Detectives secured the residence and surrounding area while requesting assistance from the Bomb Disposal Team. Bomb technicians removed seven suspected destructive devices from the home and placed them in a containment vessel. After obtaining a search warrant, deputies found and safely removed an eighth suspected explosive device, along with a large quantity of materials used to make explosive devices. Eight firearms were also seized from the home as part of the risk protection order. This investigation underscores the seriousness of what our detectives encountered and the importance of being alert to the threats around us, said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Our Targeted Violence Unit detectives recognized the potential danger and took immediate action, and our Bomb Disposal Team technicians put themselves in harm’s way to safely secure and remove these devices. I’m proud of their professionalism and courage, and grateful for the expertise and partnership of the FBI and ATF as we continue this investigation. See also: FDNY survivor recalls 9/11, shares new health battle 25 years later As a result of the investigation, Keith Anthony Morrone, 57, was charged with eight counts of possessing, making or attempting to make a destructive device. Morrone is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $20,000 bond. The investigation remains ongoing. The sheriff’s office said there is no immediate threat to the community.

Lucie County staff are providing updates to commissioners tonight on the removal of automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-maintained roads after a vote earlier this month. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said letters were sent earlier this week to all permit holders, notifying them of the decision and giving them 30 days to remove the cameras. "Earlier this week, letters went out to all the permit holders, whether some of those were permits were submitted on the behalf of law enforcement agencies, some were directly manufacturers of those cameras. So, they were notified this week and have 30 days to remove those cameras from the St. Lucie County right-of-ways," Gill said. County right-of-ways include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. Gill said there were about 50 to 55 permits issued for the cameras. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. "I'm sure the permit owners going to want to do that because...I'm sure there's value to these cameras that they don't want damaged, and they did the installations, so we're going to make sure they comply with the 30-day rule, or we'll begin the process of removing them ourselves," Gill said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. "I'm not happy about them. I think they are too intrusive and they might really impede our freedom," said Toria Hoke, a St. Another resident, Herman Felton, shared similar concerns. "I think it's a spy on the city...it's spying on the people, that's what I think it is," Felton said. However, Felton also acknowledged the cameras could be useful in certain situations. "It's good in one area, and it's not so good in another area because people have their privacy...you can't invade on their privacy. Whatever they're doing at their house is their business," he said. County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.

Students and staff at Martin County High School were evacuated Monday afternoon after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. "We are currently evacuating all buildings under the direction of the Martin County Sheriff's Office due to a bomb threat. The safety of our students and staff remains our highest priority," school officials said. The school said it is working closely with law enforcement and will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available. No injuries have been reported, and officials have not released additional details about the nature of the threat or whether any suspicious items have been found. This is the second bomb threat reported at the school this month, raising concerns among parents and school staff as authorities continue investigating the incidents. School leaders thanked families for their patience and cooperation during the evacuation and emphasized that student and staff safety remains the top priority. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is expected to provide further information as the investigation continues. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

Boca Helping Hands, Florida Atlantic University Athletics and community partners are teaming up again for the 5th annual Tackle Hunger cereal drive during the upcoming FAU-FIU Shula Bowl in Boca Raton.The event encourages fans attending Saturday’s football game at Flagler Credit Union Stadium to bring unopened boxes of cereal to help local families facing food insecurity. Fans who donate cereal will receive a free ticket to a future FAU home football game, organizers said."Believe it or not, there are 50,000 young people who go hungry every day in our community," said Dr. Andrew Hagen, CEO of Boca Helping Hands. "Of course, we want them to have enough to eat, so they can do well in school and be successful."Hagen said breakfast foods like cereal are some of the most needed — and least donated — items at food pantries."Morning breakfast is so important," Hagen said. "It's hard for families to get up and cook a full meal if they have the assets to do it, but a box of cereal worked for me when I was growing up."The cereal drive is part of Hunger Action Month efforts across South Florida aimed at raising awareness about food insecurity and increasing donations for local nonprofits.John Tull, general manager for FAU Sports Properties, said the partnership with Boca Helping Hands continues growing each year through the football program and fan support."We're proud to host this weekend the 5th annual Cereal4All food drive at the Owls game," Tull said. "Bring cereal and get a ticket to a future game. It’s that simple."Saturday’s matchup between FAU and FIU is the annual Shula Bowl rivalry game."It's winning in paradise on and off the field," Tull said. "This is a community partnership with Boca Helping Hands. We couldn't be more excited about collecting cereal this Saturday."Robes Law Group also joined the campaign this season through the "Tackle Hunger, Tackle for a Loss" initiative. The firm will donate $26 to Boca Helping Hands for every FAU tackle for loss during the football season in recognition of the Owls' 26th football season."A tackle for loss is when the defense tackles the opposing team behind the line of scrimmage,” said Thomas Robes of Robes Law Group. “For every tackle for loss, Robes Law Group is donating $26 to help with this drive."Boca Helping Hands serves more than 40,000 people annually through food assistance, workforce development and support programs across Palm Beach County.Organizers say the need for food assistance remains high as many South Florida families continue facing rising grocery and housing costs.Fans interested in supporting the cereal drive can attend the FAU-FIU game Saturday night in Boca Raton or learn more at the Boca Helping Hands Tackle Hunger website.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. In the mind of Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.It happened in May, in a far-from-filled Swedish arena, when Barkov suited up for Finland in an exhibition against Switzerland for his first game since shredding his right knee in the Panthers' first training camp practice 7 1/2 months earlier. And on one of his very first shifts, he tumbled to the ice.WATCH BELOW: Panthers ice crew preps Amerant Bank ArenaRELATED: More Florida Panthers newsNothing bad happened.“Very good news,” Barkov said.That was it. That was all it took for Barkov to realize his surgically repaired knee was good, that he could play without fear or concern. A few weeks later, he hoisted the trophy when Finland won the IIHF world championship.And now he's home in Florida, set for the start of training camp and ready to lead a team that — even after missing the playoffs last season — has been set by most sportsbooks as the favorite to win what would be its third Stanley Cup in a four-year span.“Don't take anything for granted,” Barkov said, when asked what he learned from not being able to play for Florida last season. “You just have to enjoy every single chance you get to play hockey, to be with your teammates, to go to every single practice, every single game. You’ve got to be excited about that.”The Panthers — who were holding media day on Wednesday in advance of Thursday's first practice of camp — have plenty of reasons to be excited. Many core players from the runs to the Cup titles in 2024 and 2025 are back, names like Barkov, Matthew Tkachuk, Sam Reinhart, Sam Bennett, Aaron Ekblad, Carter Verhaeghe, Gustav Forsling, Brad Marchand, Anton Lundell, Dmitry Kulikov and Niko Mikkola.Brady Tkachuk, Matthew Tkachuk's brother, has been added to the mix and Florida even brought Radko Gudas — a fan favorite from his first stint with the Panthers — back to help shore up the defense. And in net, with Sergei Bobrovsky gone to Toronto, Florida is turning the goaltender job over to Jacob Markstrom.“Every single guy who has come in, they look so determined to be their best and to show their best," Barkov said. “But they also know that we’re all in this together. Every single person is important, and every single has their own abilities to lead in their own way. We have many of those guys, so that’s the best part of this. No one’s here by themselves. Everyone can be just whatever they are.”That didn't happen last season. Injuries gutted the Panthers, starting with Barkov.He got hurt about 20 minutes into the first practice of training camp, tearing the ACL and MCL in his right knee on Sept. He had surgery a day later and was skating within a few months, but by the time he was ready to seriously consider returning to game action Florida — which dealt with injuries all year — was out of playoff contention and didn't get a chance at trying to win a third consecutive Stanley Cup.It wasn't entirely a lost season for Barkov. He missed the chance to serve as Finland's captain at the Milan Cortina Olympics, but played for his country at the IIHF world championships this past spring — and got to hoist the trophy when Finland beat host Switzerland 1-0 in the gold medal game.And now, Florida's career leader in goals and assists is raring to go with the Panthers once again.“We all know camp is always going to be hard, no matter what. It's going to be hard physically and mentally," Barkov said. "We're all kind of ready for that test.”

The WTA Finals, the elite season-ending event in women's tennis, will be held in Charlotte, North Carolina, for the next three years in a move that organizers hope will create "the Super Bowl for women's sports."The tournament will be played at the Spectrum Center, home of the NBA's Charlotte Hornets, the WTA and the Charlotte Sports Foundation announced Wednesday.The year's top eight singles players and doubles teams qualify for the event, which is usually held in November."Our ambition is for the WTA Finals to be not only the premier championship in women's tennis, but one of the defining global events in women sports," WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. "We want to create the Super Bowl for women's sports. And not just the competition, but an event that is the annual gathering for women's tennis, women's sports, and women's sport business.""Audiences are growing, investment is growing, female athletes are increasingly at the center of sports and culture around the world. And women's tennis has helped lead and define that progress for more than 50 years. And we believe our biggest championship should reflect the scale of this moment," Camillo added.Camillo called it a "minimum three-year deal. She added, "We'll see what goes on beyond that."The announcement comes at a time of financial difficulty for the WTA after it announced in July that it was opting out of the final year of a three-year hosting arrangement with Saudi Arabia to move this year's Finals to Indian Wells, California.There were concerns about going back to Saudi Arabia due to military conflicts in the Middle East.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | WTA introduces gene testing for all players on women's tennis tourCamillo noted that "2026 is a year of transition for the WTA" and that "we are doing the normal belt tightening you would expect in any business while also absorbing the unexpected cost of relocating the WTA finals to Indian Wells."What's most important to know is that we have a clear path to deliver consistent, sustainable financial performance in 2027 and beyond," she added.With Indian Wells now set to host only once, Charlotte will become the eighth different venue for the Finals since 2018.The WTA did not announce any prize money figures for the upcoming tournaments, and could struggle to match the record-setting amounts that were on offer in Saudi Arabia.Elena Rybakina collected $5.23 million for winning the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh after going 5-0 at the event. The WTA said that was the largest payout in the history of women's sports. Aryna Sabalenka earned $2.7 million as runner-up.Rybakina also beat Sabalenka in Saturday's U.S. Open final and claimed the No. 1 ranking.Coco Gauff won the 2024 finals in Riyadh.The partnership will extend beyond the Finals. The WTA will also relocate its global headquarters from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Charlotte, as part of the deal.And there's a plan to bring a WTA 500 tournament to Charlotte after 2029."The WTA has always owned the WTA finals, but now going forward, we're going to operate it too," Camillo said. "We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing."And that allows us to control our own destiny," Camillo added. "Whether it's around what we're doing with our media rights and our production, whether it's related to the WTA finals, whether we're approaching our calendar, we're going to be making bold and aggressive moves for women's tennis that shapes the future that we want rather than reacting."RELATED STORY | Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins French Open to become youngest champion since 1992Camillo replaced retiring chair Steve Simon at the end of last year.She previously oversaw business operations for the Philadelphia Flyers and Wells Fargo Center as the president and CEO of the sports and entertainment division of Comcast Spectacor, and has held senior roles with the Washington Nationals and the NBA.Asked if there was a desire to eventually merge with the ATP Finals — the men's season-ending event — Camillo said "there hasn't been an in-depth conversation about merging" the two tournaments."I think that when we create our ambition, people are going to want to merge with us on this event and many more," she added.The move to the Hornets arena during the NBA season means that the Finals will be condensed from eight to five days.That means the traditional schedule of two singles and two doubles matches per day could become four singles and four doubles matches per day."We are exploring a series of alternate formats," Camillo said.The Spectrum Center has already hosted high-profile tennis exhibition events in recent years."As an organization, our mission is quite simple," Will Pitts, CEO of the Charlotte Sports Foundation, said of the Finals. "It's drive economic impact and add to the quality of life through high-profile sporting events and unique partnerships. And this certainly does that."The move comes as Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper is investing an additional $500 million into ongoing stadium renovations with an eye toward potentially bringing the Super Bowl, NFL draft, 2031 Women's World Cup and other major sporting events to Charlotte.

A Lake Worth man is facing charges after deputies say he stole liquor from a Martin County store, then drove recklessly into Palm Beach County before being taken into custody. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, 24-year-old Derwyn Don Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. 26 and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving. A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. See also: Indian River sheriff's sergeant on leave amid Flock camera investigation Because the incident did not meet the agency’s pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. Edwards was charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

Flock cameras helped track down a burglary suspect in Vero Beach , according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office . IRCSO says that Guy Keith Tibbetts II, 44, was arrested on Sept. 6 after an allegedly burglary at a home on Reef Road in Vero Beach. According to the affidavit, deputies were called when the homeowner who was out of town at the time saw an unknown man inside of his home via his surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man, later identified as Tibbetts, wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves showing up at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed Tibbetts inside of the home with a flashlight and a tote bag. He could be seen opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door, IRCSO says. The items taking were estimated to be valued at around $1,010. See also: 'I killed my mom': No bond for man charged in mother's stabbing death in west Delray Beach Deputies collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door. Investigators also used the homeowner’s description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, the affidavit said. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to Tibbett's apartment complex. After being read his rights, Tibbetts allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission, according to the affidavit. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on reef road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage, and he was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, and grand theft between $750 and $5,000, along with another theft charge.

Lucie County sheriff is warning against handling firearms while drinking alcohol after two people were arrested over the weekend near Fort Pierce. Deputies responded to reports of individuals firing multiple weapons into the ground outside a residence in the 5100 block of Happiness Street. According to the sheriff's office, the individuals had been drinking alcohol before and during the incident. Sheriff Richard Del Toro was asked about the law. "You can discharge a firearm on your property. It's not recommended, especially in a close-type of residential type neighborhood, but again, when you're mixing alcohol, this could have ended very differently," Del Toro said. Tiffany Lindo and Jacob Mills were taken into custody, and several weapons, including a shotgun, rifle, and handguns, were seized at the scene. "It would be legal if you weren't using alcohol, but the fact that they were under the influence, that's what made it a second-degree misdemeanor," Del Toro said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates The sheriff explained that the offense could result in up to six months in jail or probation. "We want to make sure that they're being safe with firearms. You know, I'm very pro-Second Amendment, but at the same time, we have to do things responsibly, and anytime you're using alcohol, please do not use firearms," the sheriff said. No injuries were reported during the incident, but the sheriff emphasized that the innocent public is the victim in such situations. "I mean, dealing with a firearm in general can be a dangerous thing; you mix in alcohol, and it can be very dangerous for the people around there," Del Toro said. "So, the public and the state of Florida are the victim, and we have zero tolerance when it comes to doing things like that." Both Lindo and Mills have bonded out of jail. The charges they face include discharging a firearm in public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. Lucie parent is calling for changes to a school bus stop near Paar Drive and Winslow Street, saying students are forced to walk along portions of the road where there is no sidewalk. Lucie parent raises safety concerns over bus stop “This is an easy resolve, make two stops,” Green said. She tells WPTV her biggest concern is the limited space available for students walking along Paar Drive. “That's the white line for the car... that shouldn't be for a human being,” Green said. Green suggests splitting the stops in the area so students have less distance to walk along the roadway. Instead of having students use only the bus stop at Paar Drive and Winslow Street, she would like to see an additional bus stop at Paar Drive and Jarmer Road. Lucie Public Schools about Green's concerns. A long-delayed development project in downtown Fort Pierce is getting more time. City commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give the developer of King's Landing another six months to secure the additional $15 million it says it needs to build a planned $65 million Marriott hotel. The decision came after a lengthy discussion over whether the city should continue working with developer Live Oak or end the agreement. Pretty much everyone agrees Fort Pierce needs a downtown hotel. The planned project would sit along the city's waterfront and is expected to bring millions of dollars in economic activity to the area. We'd be delighted to have a Marriott here, Fort Pierce resident Charlie Hagg said. But after years of delays, some community members told commissioners they believe the city has waited long enough. "It's time to kick them to the curb," said Howard Dunn Jr. "It's time to move on, cut the losses." Others supported giving the developer another six months. Let's listen to what they have to say. Six months is not that long, Jamie Hurst said. Live Oak is planning a $65 million Marriott hotel as part of the $200 million King's Landing development. The developer told commissioners it still needs to raise another $15 million to move forward and asked for a six-month extension . Joe Collier, a hotel operating and hospitality partner, said the team will use a different approach to raising the money and needs additional time to put that plan into action. We're going to get in the trenches with Bill and help him raise the money in a different way but need time to do it, Collier said. See also: Former Palm Beach Gardens teacher gets 10 years after pleading guilty in student sex case Commissioners were divided over the future of project. The developer has already missed a key deadline under its agreement with the city, prompting some commissioners to push for termination. This is in material breach, Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said. "We need to stop now because if we do another amendment it continues to weaken us." Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that ending the agreement could create even more delays, including the possibility of another round of negotiations with a new developer and a lengthy legal battle. If we pull the plug on this deal now, we're looking at 10 years of turnaround time before we're going to have anything completed over there, Broderick said. "This project is integrally critical to the City of Fort Pierce. "We need a downtown hotel. We need more downtown retail." Commissioners ultimately voted 3-2 to give Live Oak six more months to secure the additional $15 million. The citizens of City of Fort Pierce do not want to wait 10 years. They want this done now, Broderick said. A new agreement will be drafted over the next 30 days. Then, Live Oak will have six months to secure the additional funding needed for the hotel. If the project stays on track, city leaders say construction could begin in roughly one to one-and-a-half years.

A Lake Worth man is facing charges after deputies say he stole liquor from a Martin County store, then drove recklessly into Palm Beach County before being taken into custody. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, 24-year-old Derwyn Don Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. 26 and stole multiple bottles of liquor. We're now a few weeks into the new school year and we're highlighting the amazing things teachers are doing in the lives of your students. CBS12 News’ next Teacher Feature within the Martin County School District is said to be a great model for the relatively new co-teaching initiative being rolled out at certain schools. Kevin Kobold is a geometry co-teacher at South Fork High School in Stuart. "Okay, so like usually there's like 28 to 29 kids in the classroom. So if there's one teacher trying to instruct to 29 minds in there, you might lose half of them. So if we split it in half, and now it's a ratio of like 15 to one, you're really able to engage with the students more and really like focus on some kids that are struggling, said Kabold. "I'm helping take a lot off her weight that she doesn't have to be up there instructing from bell to bell every class. I can be doing the same thing too. So, getting to know your co-teacher and knowing your role in the classroom, I think, is key there. And also being able to like finish each other's sentences, like what we do in there." Kabold knows geometry can be difficult to a lot of students and really focuses on making his lessons interesting and fun, rather than just note-taking. "So, if we're working on notes, they're usually like guided notes where they're not having to write two pages of their own handwriting. That's when you'll lose a lot of the kids. So we use the whiteboards. We have stations set up, said Kabold. "We're reviewing for a test on Friday, so we're really having them engage with the material to try to get it to stick a little more than just sitting there and doing a review on the computer." See also: 'We were ready': One family's journey to keeping foster brothers together District officials said that students really respect Kabold, which he says is really important to gain early on. "I mean, like when you gain that rapport with students, and they kind of find out that you're there for them and you truly do care about them, they will open up a little more, and they will try harder than just you know sitting back there and not asking them about, 'Hey how'd your football game go?' Or, 'hey how'd your band practice go?' said Kabold. Like once you get to know them and know what they do out of the classroom, then you see like their eyes light up, and now they want to come in class." Kabold says while he knows geometry isn’t the most fun class, there is one big message he wants his students to leave with. "If you learn some geometry, that's amazing. I want you to do well on your EOC. But this is really about solving problems that come up in your life when you're given certain information. How am I going to solve this problem? I really try to make it real life for them because let's be real, a lot of them may not have a career that requires them to remember the Pythagorean theorem or something from geometry, but they're going to be faced with issues in their life, and I don't want them to just hide from them. So just try in our classroom, be present, and you'll learn something. I promise." Co-teaching has been used in Martin County middle and high school over the past few years. This is only the second year at South Fork High. District officials say co-teaching is about to be introduced in elementary schools, but didn't specify when. A more unsettled weather pattern is setting up across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches for the middle and latter part of the week, bringing elevated chances for showers and thunderstorms, breezy northeast winds and a growing risk of rougher conditions at the beaches. An upper-level low approaching Florida from the western Atlantic is the feature behind the change. In simple terms, it will add energy higher in the atmosphere while pulling in deep tropical moisture at lower levels. That combination should make it easier for showers and storms to develop not just during the typical afternoon window, but at times earlier or later in the day as well. Wednesday will feature a mix of sun and clouds, with scattered showers and thunderstorms becoming more likely through the afternoon and evening. High temperatures will still reach the upper 80s to around 90 degrees, so it will remain warm and humid despite the increase in clouds and rain chances. Heat indices look to be a few degrees below the triple digits to near 100 degrees, a few degrees cooler than recently. A few storms could produce frequent lightning, brief heavy downpours and gusty winds. The storm coverage is expected to increase further Thursday and Friday as the upper-level low moves closer to the peninsula. Rain chances are elevated across both the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with numerous showers and thunderstorms possible at times. This does not mean the entire area will see nonstop rain or a complete washout, but outdoor plans could face interruptions, especially during the afternoon and evening. The main concern will be pockets of heavy rain. Storms may move slowly at times or repeatedly affect the same locations, raising the risk for localized street flooding and ponding water in poor-drainage areas. The severe-weather threat appears low overall, but isolated stronger storms could still bring gusty winds and plenty of cloud-to-ground lightning. Breezy easterly to northeasterly winds will also become more noticeable, particularly near the coast. Those winds may offer only limited relief from the humidity while creating choppier conditions along the Atlantic waters. For boaters, a Small Craft Advisory is in effect from this afternoon through late tonight for the entire Treasure Coast and Palm Beach coastal waters. Northeast to east winds are expected to increase to 15 to 20 knots, while seas build to 4 to 6 feet, occasionally reaching 8 feet offshore. Conditions in the Intracoastal Waterway will also become choppy in exposed areas. Beachgoers should use extra caution as the onshore flow increases. The National Weather Service has posted a Rip Current Statement for Atlantic beaches. Increasing onshore wind and building surf can create dangerous currents that pull swimmers away from shore, even when the weather appears calm between showers. By the weekend, the upper-level low should begin shifting west, allowing the weather pattern to gradually return toward more typical scattered afternoon storms.

Lucie County Sheriff’s Office arrested a Fort Pierce man after an investigation that began Thursday identified suspected destructive devices at a residence. Keith Anthony Morrone, 57, of Fort Pierce, was arrested and charged with eight counts of explosives, possessing, making or attempting to make destructive devices, the sheriff's office said Friday. The home is in the 6000 block of Balsam Drive. Morrone is currently being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $20,000 bond. At approximately 12:20 p.m. Thursday, detectives with the SLCSO Targeted Violence Unit were serving a risk protection order at the residence when they identified suspected destructive devices, Fort Pierce police said in a news release Friday morning. Detectives secured the residence and surrounding area and requested assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Bomb Disposal Team. Bomb technicians also responded to the residence and conducted a preliminary examination of the suspected devices. Technicians removed seven devices from the residence and safely secured them in a containment vessel. Detectives subsequently obtained a search warrant for the residence. During the execution of the search warrant, investigators located an additional improvised explosive device, which was safely secured and removed. This brought the total number of improvised explosive devices recovered from the residence to eight. Investigators also found a large quantity of materials used in the construction of explosive devices. Eight firearms were also taken into custody pursuant to the service of a risk protection order. “This investigation underscores the seriousness of what our detectives encountered and the importance of being alert to the threats around us,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said. “Our Targeted Violence Unit detectives recognized the potential danger and took immediate action, and our Bomb Disposal Team technicians put themselves in harm’s way to safely secure and remove these devices. I’m proud of their professionalism and courage, and grateful for the expertise and partnership of the FBI and ATF as we continue this investigation.” The investigation remains ongoing, and there is no immediate threat to the community. “They came across a box of items that were indicative of being destructive devices,” said Capt. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Neighbors expressed concern about the situation. “That’s really bad,” Terry Rates, who has lived in the neighborhood for 10 years, told WPBF's Ari Hait. Rates described the area as peaceful and said he was surprised to see such activity near his home. “It’s a really nice neighborhood. That’s the first I’ve ever heard of anything happening around here,” he said. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.
